How a job runs

From the first telephone call to the last signature, a job with ATKAYVA passes through the same eleven steps. Small jobs pass through them in a day. Large ones take months. The steps do not change.

Under pressure

Before the order

  1. You tell us what must be done

    By telephone, by message or on the enquiry page. Plain words are enough. We ask what, where, by when, and who we should speak to.

  2. We come and look

    No decision about a site is made by someone who has not seen it. We walk the job with your engineer, look at the ground, the access, the neighbouring plant and the route for machines. We ask about permits, isolations and working hours.

  3. We make an offer

    The scope as we understand it, written out. The price, with its basis. The time we need. What we assume, and what we need from you. If we cannot meet the date safely, the offer says so.

  4. You place the order

    A work order, a rate contract call-off or a contract, as your system requires. See Ways to engage us.

Phase one. Task acceptance and scoping

  1. A project manager is named

    One person who answers to you from this day until the handover, with authority to deploy what the job needs.

  2. The kick-off

    A short meeting at the site. Drawings, the baseline schedule, the permit system, gate formalities, emergency arrangements and the reporting format are agreed. The names and numbers of both sides are exchanged.

Phase two. Resource orchestration

  1. The network is called

    Machines, people, materials, transport and engineering support are booked against the schedule. You approve none of it. You see none of it.

  2. People and machines are cleared

    Medicals, gate passes and inductions for people. Papers and inspection for machines and vehicles. This is done before the start date, not on it.

Phase three. Execution with embedded quality

  1. The work is done

    Under your permit to work, with our supervisors on every shift. Each stage is offered for inspection before the next begins. You receive one progress report a day.

Phase four. Handover and site closure

  1. Inspection, snags and cleaning

    The finished work is inspected jointly. Snags are listed and cleared. The site is cleaned: scrap, scaffold, tools and temporary works all leave. Permits are closed.

  2. The handover file and the invoice

    Test reports, inspection records, as-built drawings and measurement sheets, in one file. Then one invoice, with the records behind it.

And afterwards

We come back. If something we built gives trouble, the telephone number is the same and so are the people. A firm that lives a few kilometres from your gate cannot hide from its own work, and would not wish to.

The whole of it, on one page

You do
Say what must be done. Show us the site. Issue permits and isolations. Inspect at each stage. Accept the work.
We do
Everything else.
You receive
One name. One schedule. One report a day. One handover file. One invoice.

One accountable face

The project manager assigned to a client is the single accountable face of ATKAYVA on that job.

That person holds the authority to deploy network resources at once, without escalation and without waiting on a head office. The structure is flat by intent. A firm that sells speed cannot afford to have that speed blunted by its own bureaucracy.

The cadence

A baseline schedule, with resources
Agreed before work begins. Every activity has a duration, a sequence and the people and machines it needs.
Daily progress monitoring
Planned against done, activity by activity, with corrective action the same day.
A daily report
Sent to you at the end of each day. See the specimen below.
A weekly review
With your team. It is optional, and clients often waive it once trust is established.
A handover package
Assembled as the work is done.

The daily progress report

It is the only thing that reaches your desk, so it has to carry everything you need and nothing you do not.

ATKAYVA

Daily progress report

SPECIMEN
Job
Raw mill hopper foundation and trench
Day
14 of 32
Done today
Raft reinforcement completed and offered for inspection. Trench excavation, chainage 60 to 95 m, in rock.
Planned tomorrow
Raft pour, 180 m³, starting 20:00. Trench, chainage 95 to 120 m.
On site today
1 engineer, 2 supervisors, 38 workers. 2 excavators with breakers, 1 crane, 4 tippers.
Inspections
Request raised for raft reinforcement. Signed 16:40.
Safety
Toolbox talk held. No incident. One observation closed: barricade at trench crossing.
At risk

Needed from you

Specimen

Read the last two lines again. At risk tells you what might go wrong before it has. Needed from you is short, specific and has a time on it. If that line is ever long, we are not doing our job.

Requests for inspection

Nothing is buried, covered or built upon until it has been seen.

Every stage that will be hidden by the next is offered to your engineer on a request for inspection: founding levels, reinforcement, embedments, alignment before grouting, surface preparation before painting. The request is raised in time for you to attend. The signed sheet goes into the handover file.

When the scope changes

Jobs change. Rock appears where soil was expected. A crack is longer than it looked. You decide to add a platform while we are there.

  1. We tell you before, not after

    What has been found or asked for, what it will take and what it will cost, at the rates in the order or at rates we propose.

  2. You decide

    In writing. A message from an authorised person is enough.

  3. It is recorded

    Measured jointly and listed separately in the bill.

We do not discover extra work and present it at the end.

When something is going wrong

  1. The supervisor on shift

    Settles it on the spot wherever possible. Has the authority to stop a job.

  2. The project manager

    Reachable by you at any hour. Can deploy more people, another machine or a different method without asking anyone.

  3. The leadership

    Reachable by the project manager at any hour, and by you whenever you wish. Their number is the firm’s number.

Three rungs, and no more. If a problem has to climb higher than that to be solved, the firm is too tall.

Records

During the job
Schedule updates, daily reports, attendance, machine hours, inspection requests, test results, permits and toolbox talk records.
At handover
Test certificates, signed inspections, as-built drawings, measurement sheets and the snag list, closed.
Afterwards
Kept by us and available to you.

Some clients want a foundation. Some want twelve fitters until Sunday. Some want never to think about buses again. There are six ways to contract with us, and the right one depends on the work.

Six models

Work orders and item-rate contracts
For a defined civil or mechanical scope. The work is listed as items, each with a rate. You pay for the quantity measured.
Annual rate contracts
For recurring maintenance, civil repairs and services. Rates are agreed once, and jobs are called off through the year. See Annual rate contracts.
Shutdown and turnaround packages
Manpower, machinery and logistics for a fixed window, against a job list. See Planned shutdowns.
Composite packages
Civil, mechanical, haulage and manpower combined under one order. See The whole job, one order.
Hire
Machinery, transport and fleet, by the shift, the month or the year, always with operator or driver.
Emergency call-out
At any hour. At agreed rates if you hold a rate contract with us, and at our standard call-out rates if you do not.

Which one fits

AspectIf your situation is thisConsider this
A structure to be built to a drawingItem-rate work order
Many small jobs you cannot predictAnnual rate contract
The kiln stops on a known dateShutdown package
A project with several kinds of workComposite package
You have the crew and need a machineHire
Your own maintenance team needs more handsManpower under a rate contract
The plant is down tonightCall. We will settle the paper in the morning.

What we need in order to price

Send what you have. We will ask for the rest.

For a fuller request, use the request for quotation page.

What our offer contains

  • The scope, as we understand it, in our own words
  • Rates or prices, and what each includes
  • The time we need and the resources we will deploy
  • What we have assumed
  • What we need from you
  • Validity, and tax as applicable

We do not price a job low in the hope of recovering through extras. An offer that looks cheap and ends expensive is the surest way to be the second number a client dials.

Commercial hygiene

Measurement
Joint, at site, as work proceeds.
Records
Attendance and machine hours signed each shift.
Tax
Tax invoices as the law requires.
Payment
To the firm’s bank account only, as notified on our letterhead. See Fraud alert.
Gifts and favours
We neither offer nor accept anything that could influence a contract. See Anti-bribery and gifts.

Ready to ask for a price?

One line per item is enough to begin.

Before we are a vendor

  1. Registration

    Your vendor system wants our statutory papers, bank details and declarations. We send them in your format. See Document requests and Becoming our client.

  2. Pre-qualification

    Your safety and quality teams want to know how we work. We answer the questionnaire, show the records behind our figures and, if you wish, take you to a site where we are working.

  3. A first conversation

    With someone who can decide. See Leadership.

Before we enter the plant

Every plant controls who and what comes through its gate. We prepare for that before the start date.

For each person
Identity and address proof. Police verification where the plant asks for it. A medical fitness certificate, and a separate one for work at height. Evidence of skill for the trade. Our own induction, then yours.
For each machine and vehicle
Registration, insurance, fitness and pollution certificates. Operator’s or driver’s licence. For lifting equipment, a current test certificate. An inspection by your safety team.
For tools and tackle
Portable electrical tools inspected and tagged. Slings and shackles certified. Gas cylinders with caps, gauges and flashback arrestors.
For the job
A method statement and risk assessment for the work, in your format if you have one.

The kick-off

One meeting, at the site, before the first day of work.

Kick-off agenda

The first week

The first week sets the tone for the years that follow. We know what you are watching for.

Do they come when they said?
Yes.
Do they follow our rules without being reminded?
They were told the rules before they arrived.
Does the supervisor know what is happening?
The supervisor is the one making it happen.
Do they tell us about a problem, or hide it?
The daily report has a line for it.
Is the site clean at the end of the shift?
Every shift.

After the first job

Most of our clients began with one small order. Inducted people stay inducted. Registered machines stay registered. The second job starts faster than the first, and the tenth faster still.

The shutdown playbook

A shutdown is the same discipline as an emergency, with a calendar attached. It is won in the six weeks before the kiln goes cold, by people with clipboards walking the plant and asking awkward questions.

4 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. Five principles
  2. The countdown
  3. The job card
  4. The daily rhythm
  5. Found work
  6. What we ask of the plant
  7. Safety in a shutdown
How we work
  • How we work overview

The method

  • How a job runs
  • Project governance
  • Ways to engage us
  • Starting with a new client

Under pressure

  • The shutdown playbook
  • The emergency protocol
  • Proximity

Five principles

  1. The date of light-up is the only date

    Every job is planned backwards from the day the plant must run again.

  2. Nothing starts on day one that could have started before

    Scaffold, staging of material, inductions and prefabrication all happen while the plant is still running.

  3. Every job has an owner, a crew and a place in the queue

    A job without all three is a wish.

  4. Found work is certain

    Something will be discovered when the plant is opened. People and time are held in reserve for it.

  5. Safety gets harder, not easier

    More people, more permits, more work overhead. The system must be strongest when the pressure is highest.

The countdown

  1. T − 6 weeks

    Walk the scope

    With your engineers, job by job, on the plant. For each job we record what is to be done, where, the access, the isolations, the permits, the lifting, the material and who supplies it.

  2. T − 5 weeks

    Write the job list

    One line per job, with a number. This list is the shutdown. If a job is not on it, it does not exist.

  3. T − 4 weeks

    Load the schedule

    Durations, sequence and resources. Jobs that share a crane, a platform or a vessel are put in order. The longest chain of jobs is found, because that chain sets the light-up date.

  4. T − 3 weeks

    Book the network

    Crews by trade and shift are called from the register. Cranes, machines, tippers and buses are reserved. Medicals and gate passes begin.

  5. T − 2 weeks

    Prefabricate and procure

    Anything that can be cut, welded or assembled in advance is. Consumables are counted. Long-delivery items are chased.

  6. T − 1 week

    Stage and induct

    Material is placed at the work fronts. Scaffold that can be built with the plant running is built. Everyone is inducted. Supervisors walk their jobs again.

  7. Day 0

    Kiln off

    The plant cools and isolates. Areas are handed to us under permit, one at a time.

  8. Days 1 to n

    Run the plan

    Three shifts. One coordination meeting a day. One report a day.

  9. Light-up − 2 days

    Close out

    Tools counted. Scaffold struck. Debris cleared. Permits closed. Areas handed back.

  10. Light-up

    Stand by

    A crew remains through start-up for the leak, the loose bolt and the guard that rubs.

  11. + 1 week

    Review

    What went well, what did not, and what will be done differently next year, written down while it is fresh.

Sketch your own countdown with the shutdown planner.

The job card

ATKAYVA

Shutdown job card

SPECIMEN
Job number
M-27
Job
Replace dip tube, cyclone 3
Location
Preheater, level 5
Planned
Days 3 to 6, three shifts
Crew per shift
1 supervisor, 4 fitters, 2 welders, 4 riggers, 4 helpers
Equipment
Crane on days 3 and 5. Chain blocks. Welding sets.
Permits
Confined space. Hot work. Work at height.
Precondition
Cyclone cleaned and build-up above removed. Scaffold inspected.
Depends on
Job M-25, which uses the same crane
Hold point
Inspection of fit-up before welding
Specimen

The daily rhythm

Start of each shift
Toolbox talk by job. Permits revalidated. Handover from the outgoing supervisor, at the work front and not in the office.
Mid-morning
The coordination meeting. Every job: planned, actual, blocked or clear. Fifteen minutes, standing.
Through the day
Supervisors report progress and found work as it happens.
End of day
The daily report. The plan for tomorrow, adjusted for what today taught.

Found work

Open a cyclone and you may find a crack nobody knew about. This is not a failure of planning. It is why the plant was opened.

  • It is reported at once, with photographs.
  • Your engineer decides whether it is done now or deferred.
  • It gets a job number, a crew from the reserve and a place in the schedule.
  • It is priced at the rates agreed before the shutdown began.

What we ask of the plant

With these, a shutdown runs. Without them, it waits.

Safety in a shutdown

Everything on Life-saving rules applies, and three things matter more than usual.

Work above work
Jobs are sequenced so that nobody works beneath another crew. Where it cannot be avoided, decks and nets are fitted.
Fatigue
Shifts are rotated and rest days are real. Nobody works a double shift on a job that can hurt them.
Strangers
A shutdown brings many people who have not worked together. Every crew has a core of people who know the plant.

Give us the date

Six weeks before the kiln goes cold is the right time to call. Earlier is better.

Request a shutdown packageUse the planner

A teacher for this page

Leo Tolstoy

The novel, 1828 to 1910

In How Much Land Does a Man Need? a peasant is promised all the land he can walk around between sunrise and sunset. He walks too far, runs back as the light goes, and falls dead at the finish. His servant buries him in six feet of ground, which turns out to be all he needed.

What we tookA shutdown is the same bargain: a fixed sunset, and a list of work that always wants to grow. Our playbook freezes the list before the first day, so that the plant lights up on time.

Is something down now?

Call the site office. The number is on the Contact page. Read this later.

What to tell us

Minute 0. The call

The telephone is answered by a person. We ask five questions, and we ask them in the same order every time.

  1. Which plant, and which gate?

  2. Where inside?

  3. What has happened?

  4. What do you need first?

  5. Who do we ask for, and on what number?

That is all. We do not ask for a purchase order. We do not ask for a scope.

Minutes 1 to 5. Three calls

The supervisor
Someone who lives near your gate and has worked inside your plant. This person leaves at once and takes charge on arrival.
The machine
An owner-operator whose machine of the right class is parked nearby and who gives our calls priority.
The crew
Fitters, welders, riggers or a civil gang, as the problem demands.

A fourth call goes to the project manager for your account, if that is not the person who answered.

Minutes 5 to 30. Convergence

People and machines travel a few kilometres on roads they drive every day. If the machine must come on a low-loader, the low-loader is called in the first five minutes too.

While they travel we send you a short message with the name and number of the supervisor who is coming and the registration numbers of the vehicles. If your gate needs names in advance, it has them.

Arrival. Assess before acting

  1. Report

    Our supervisor reports to your shift in-charge and to no one else.

  2. Look

    At the failure, and at everything round it. What is still loaded, still hot, still live, still hanging?

  3. Agree

    What will be done first, by whom, and what the plant must isolate.

  4. Permit

    The permit to work is raised and issued. Isolations are applied by the plant, verified by us and locked.

  5. Brief

    A toolbox talk at the work front, under whatever light there is.

Only then is a tool lifted. On a well-run plant this takes minutes. It is never skipped.

The work

The network fills in behind the first responders: the second machine, more welders, material, lighting, transport to clear debris as it comes out.

Your control room receives short, factual updates from one voice, at intervals you choose. It does not receive requests for decisions that are ours to make.

Restart

We stay until the plant is running and your shift in-charge releases us. Guards go back. Tools are counted. The area is cleaned. The permit is closed.

The next morning

A report
What failed, what we did, what we used, and what we think should be looked at before it fails again.
An invoice
Hours, machines and material, at agreed rates.
A conversation
If the failure points to something larger, we say so.

What we will not do, even in an emergency

Danger

No work without a permit

પરમિટ વગર કામ નહીં

परमिट के बिना काम नहीं

Danger

No entry without isolation

आइसोलेशन के बिना प्रवेश नहीं

Danger

No entry under hanging material

લટકતા મટીરિયલ નીચે પ્રવેશ નહીં

लटकती सामग्री के नीचे प्रवेश नहीं

No production loss is worth a life. Our supervisors are instructed to refuse an unsafe instruction, and the leadership will stand behind any supervisor who does.

Ten minutes now saves twenty at midnight

Proximity as a competitive weapon

In heavy industry, time is not money. Time is production, and lost production is never recovered. A kiln that stands cold for a shift does not make those tonnes back tomorrow. A berth that waits on a repair loses the ship.

3 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. When minutes define millions
  2. What proximity saves
  3. What proximity knows
  4. Near, and distant
  5. The proximity doctrine
  6. The honest limit
How we work
  • How we work overview

The method

  • How a job runs
  • Project governance
  • Ways to engage us
  • Starting with a new client

Under pressure

  • The shutdown playbook
  • The emergency protocol

When minutes define millions

Our operating radius is small by design and enormous in its effect.

minutes to site for an emergency call-out
< 30
mobilisation distance from the core plants
0 km
of accumulated knowledge of this terrain
10 years

Contractors based in distant cities work with mobilisation windows of six to twelve hours. Our teams, and our partners’ machines, are embedded inside the industrial zone itself.

During that breakdown our civil and mechanical teams were on site within 25 minutes of the call. A competitor mobilising from outside the belt would have needed at least five hours. The plant resumed production eight hours ahead of its projected recovery.

This is not an anecdote. It is the predictable outcome of being local on purpose. The case note is at A kiln breakdown.

What proximity saves

Transport of machines
No low-loader hauling an excavator across the state and back.
Allowances
No overnight allowances for labour brought from far away.
Waiting
No productivity lost while a rental fleet is still on the highway.
Risk in the schedule
A date that depends on a convoy arriving is weaker than one that does not.

Our location takes whole lines out of a tender’s cost sheet while making its schedule more reliable.

What proximity knows

Speed is the visible half of the advantage. The other half is a decade of intimacy with this particular ground.

The rock
The basalt strata, the limestone above them and the dykes that cross both. Excavation plans anticipate the fractured interfaces before the first bucket bites.
The water
Seasonal drainage patterns. Which ground holds water and which sheds it.
The air
A salt-laden atmosphere that accelerates corrosion. Concrete mixes account for chloride before the first formwork is placed.
The plants
Which gate, which weighbridge, which permit desk. Supervisors arrive already knowing the client’s plant as well as their own backyard.
The roads
Which one floods in July.
The people
Who can weld, who can rig, and who will answer a telephone at two in the morning.

The proximity doctrine

The honest limit

Proximity is an advantage inside the belt, and we do not pretend it travels. For work beyond this district we mobilise like anyone else, and we say so in the offer. What we carry with us then is the method and the people, not the thirty minutes.

A teacher for this page

Albert Einstein

Theoretical physics, 1879 to 1955

In 1905 he was a patent examiner in Bern, checking other people’s inventions. In his own hours that year he published four papers that rebuilt physics. One of them showed that time is not the same for everyone. It depends on where you stand and how you are moving.

What we tookOn a stopped kiln, time also depends on where you stand. A crew twenty-five minutes away and a crew five hours away are not living in the same emergency.
